title: Read a language before solving it
summary: Identify the alphabet, order, counts and boundary cases before building a grammar or machine.
goals: Read set-builder notation aloud.
Distinguish the empty string from the empty language.
Separate order requirements from counting requirements.
Test examples and counterexamples systematically.

sections.title: The complete task
sections.html:
A language is a set of strings. A grammar generates strings in that set; an automaton decides whether an input string belongs to that set. Start with the language itself: what symbols may occur, in what order, and with what relationships between their counts?

For example, L = {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0} contains one block of zeros followed by an equally long block of ones. Examples include ε, 01 and 0011. The string 0101 has equal counts, but its order is wrong.

sections.title: Read each symbol
sections.html:
NotationRead it asExample
ΣThe alphabet: the available symbolsΣ = {0,1}
Σ*All finite strings over Σ, including εε, 0, 1, 00, 01, …
εThe empty string; its length is zero0⁰ = ε
∅The empty set: a language containing no stringsε ∉ ∅
ε ∈ {ε}The empty string belongs to the set containing the empty string{ε} has one element
w ∈ LThe string w is a member of L0011 ∈ L
|w|The length of w|001| = 3
|w|ₐThe number of occurrences of a in w|abaca|ₐ = 3
wᴿThe reverse of w(001)ᴿ = 100
:Such that{0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}

0ⁿ means n copies of the symbol 0. It is repetition notation, not numerical exponentiation. Unless a language says otherwise, exponents here are nonnegative integers.

sections.title: Keep order and counts separate
sections.html:
0ⁿ1ᵐ imposes the order: first zeros, then ones. A condition such as n = m then constrains the two block lengths. In contrast, {w ∈ {a,b}* : |w|ₐ = |w|ᵦ} permits interleaving. It contains abba, baba and ba.

For several blocks, write a count table before constructing anything. In aⁱbʲcᵏ, the exponents belong to a, b and c respectively. Every inequality must be translated into a specific relationship.

sections.title: Why context-free languages appear
sections.html:
Unbounded nesting, such as balanced parentheses, needs more than the finite memory of a finite automaton. A context-free grammar can generate matching structure recursively. A pushdown automaton adds a stack to recognize such structure.

Every regular language is context-free. Some context-free languages are not regular, such as {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}. Some languages are not context-free. A pattern that looks like a dependency is a useful design clue, but it is not a test that proves a language context-free.

worked.title: Classify strings in a two-block language
worked.intro: Use L = {aⁱbʲ : i ≥ 1 and j = 2i}. Decide whether aabbbb belongs.

steps.title: Read the definition
steps.html: There must be at least one a. All a symbols precede all b symbols. The b block is twice as long as the a block.

steps.title: Check the alphabet and order
steps.html: aabbbb uses only a and b, with no a after the first b. It has the required two-block form.

steps.title: Count and substitute
steps.html: The counts are i = 2 and j = 4. The conditions become 2 ≥ 1 and 4 = 2·2, both true.

steps.title: Test boundary and nearby failures
steps.html: Therefore aabbbb ∈ L. The shortest member is abb. The empty string fails i ≥ 1; aabb fails the ratio; abbabb fails the order even though its total counts have the right ratio.

practice.prompt: For L = {0ⁿ1ᵐ : n < m}, classify ε, 1, 00111 and 01011.
practice.hint: Check order before the inequality. A zero-length block is allowed unless excluded.
practice.solution: ε: no, 0 < 0 is false. 1: yes, n = 0 and m = 1. 00111: yes, 2 < 3. 01011: no, a zero occurs after a one, so it is not a string of the form 0ⁿ1ᵐ.

practice.prompt: Let w = abaca. Find |w|, |w|ₐ, |w|ᵦ and wᴿ. Explain why ε and ∅ cannot be used interchangeably.
practice.hint: Reverse symbol order; do not sort the symbols.
practice.solution: The answers are 5, 3, 1 and acaba. ε is one string of length zero. ∅ is a set with no strings. A machine may accept ε, but it does not read ∅ as an input string.

check.prompt: Does 0101 belong to {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}? Explain the decisive condition.
check.answer: No. It violates the block order.
check.explanation: The zero after the first one breaks the required 0*1* form. Equal counts alone are insufficient.

transfer.prompt: Define a language of three blocks of a, b and c where the first and third blocks are nonempty and equally long, and the middle block can have any length. Give three members and three nonmembers, explaining each failure.
transfer.solution: L = {aⁱbʲcⁱ : i ≥ 1, j ≥ 0}. Members: ac, abc, aabbbcc. Nonmembers: ε (nonempty outer blocks required), aabc (outer counts differ), abac (block order fails).

title: Read and run a context-free grammar
summary: Understand the four parts of a CFG and exactly what a production permits.
goals: Identify terminals, variables, productions and the start symbol.
Read alternatives, recursion and epsilon productions.
Apply one production to exactly one variable occurrence.
Distinguish syntax from meaning.

sections.title: A complete grammar first
sections.html:
S → 0S1 | ε

Start with S. Either replace S with 0S1, adding one zero before it and one one after it, or replace S with ε, removing the remaining S. This grammar generates exactly {0ⁿ1ⁿ : n ≥ 0}.

The vertical bar means alternative productions. S → 0S1 | ε abbreviates two rules: S → 0S1 and S → ε.

sections.title: The four parts of G = (V, Σ, P, S)
sections.html:
PartMeaningFor this grammar
VVariables, also called nonterminals{S}
ΣTerminals: the actual symbols of output strings{0,1}
PThe production rules{S → 0S1, S → ε}
SThe selected start variableS

V and Σ are disjoint. ε is not a terminal symbol; it denotes a string with no symbols. An ε production is allowed even though ε is not in Σ.

Every production has exactly one variable on the left. Its right side may contain terminals, variables, both, or no symbols. A rule AB → a is not a context-free production because its left side contains two variables.

sections.title: What “context-free” means
sections.html:
If X → ρ is a rule, an occurrence of X may be replaced by ρ regardless of what is immediately before or after it. In αXβ, only the chosen X changes: the result is αρβ.

Do not replace all identical variables at once. With S → SS, the sentential form SS contains two separate occurrences. Replacing the left occurrence using S → a produces aS, not aa.

sections.title: Tokens, spelling and meaning
sections.html:
In a programming grammar, id represents a token category. cursor and result may both be id tokens, with different lexemes. Punctuation such as (, ), { and , is terminal syntax.

A grammar checks structure. A syntactically valid statement need not make semantic sense: a grammar may generate an expression that refers to an undeclared name. Similarly, an English grammar can generate a grammatical but implausible sentence.

BNF often writes ::= in place of →. Optional or repeated components in extended notation must ultimately be understood as explicit alternatives and recursion.

worked.title: Explain every part of a small list grammar
worked.intro: Use S → [ L ], L → ε | id T, T → ε | , id T. The target token sequence is [ id , id ].

steps.title: Separate the symbols
steps.html: The variables are S, L and T. The terminals are [, ], id and ,. S is the start symbol.

steps.title: Expand the fixed outside structure
steps.html: S ⇒ [ L ]. The brackets are now fixed terminals; only L can be rewritten.

steps.title: Choose a nonempty list and one additional item
steps.html: [ L ] ⇒ [ id T ] ⇒ [ id , id T ]. The tail rule adds a comma and another id.

steps.title: End the recursion
steps.html: Use T → ε: [ id , id T ] ⇒ [ id , id ]. ε contributes no printed symbol. Using L → ε instead at the earlier point would have generated the empty list [ ].

practice.prompt: For A → aA | b, identify V, Σ, P and the start symbol. Give the shortest member and two longer members.
practice.hint: The variable is a placeholder; the lowercase symbols remain in the output.
practice.solution: V = {A}, Σ = {a,b}, P = {A → aA, A → b}, start A. The shortest member is b; longer examples are ab and aab. The grammar never generates ε because there is no terminating empty production.

practice.prompt: Are X → ε, X → aYX, XY → a and a → X valid CFG productions when X,Y are variables and a is a terminal?
practice.hint: A context-free production must have one variable as its whole left side.
practice.solution: The first two are valid. XY → a has two variables on the left. a → X has a terminal on the left. Neither is a CFG production.

check.prompt: When S → ε is used inside 0S1, what string remains?
check.explanation: Only the occurrence of S is removed. The surrounding terminals remain unchanged.

transfer.prompt: Write a CFG for a bracketed, comma-separated list of zero or more integer tokens. Explain why [ , integer ] and [ integer , ] are excluded.
transfer.solution:
List → [ Items ]
Items → ε | integer Tail
Tail → ε | , integer Tail

A comma appears only through Tail → , integer Tail, so every comma must have a preceding item and a following integer. The empty option belongs to the complete list content or the remaining tail.

title: Build derivations one rule at a time
summary: Turn a target string into an explicit sequence of justified replacements.
goals: Read ⇒ and ⇒* accurately.
Identify a sentential form and a completed derivation.
Construct leftmost and rightmost derivations.
Use the terminal prefix to detect incorrect choices.

sections.title: Derivation, sentential form and membership
sections.html:
A derivation is a sequence of rule applications beginning with the start variable. A sentential form is any string of terminals and variables reached in that sequence. When no variables remain, it is a generated terminal string.

α ⇒ β means one rule application takes α to β. α ⇒* β means zero or more applications. The star includes zero steps: S ⇒* S is true. Membership is defined by L(G) = {w ∈ Σ* : S ⇒* w}.

A derivation proves a particular string belongs. Giving several examples does not prove the grammar generates exactly a proposed language; that stronger statement needs both directions, developed in the grammar-design lesson.

sections.title: Keep the whole current string visible
sections.html:
S → aSb | ε
S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aaaSbbb ⇒ aaabbb

Each arrow changes one occurrence. The last step uses S → ε. It does not erase any existing a or b.

Write the current sentential form after every replacement. Beside it, record the rule used when the derivation is long. Do not jump from one line to another by silently applying several rules.

sections.title: Leftmost and rightmost are replacement orders
sections.html:
A leftmost derivation always expands the leftmost remaining variable. A rightmost derivation always expands the rightmost remaining variable. “Leftmost” does not mean replace the first character; it means find the first variable when reading from the left.

E → E + T | T
T → T * F | F
F → number | ( E )

In E + T, a leftmost derivation expands E next; a rightmost derivation expands T next. Both can produce the same parse tree. Different expansion orders alone do not make a grammar ambiguous.

sections.title: Read target structure before choosing a rule
sections.html:
For an expression, identify the outermost operation, excluding operators inside parentheses. For (2 + 5) * 8, multiplication is outside the parentheses, so begin with a structure that has multiplication at its root.

For a list or program, identify its fixed punctuation first, then expand the parts inside it. A terminal already placed in the wrong position cannot later be rewritten away. A premature wrong terminal is a reason to revise the preceding production choice.

worked.title: Leftmost and rightmost derivations of 2 + 3 * 4
worked.intro: Use E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → number | ( E ). Treat 2,3,4 as number tokens with their lexemes shown.

steps.title: Identify the outer structure
steps.html: The top-level addition splits the expression into 2 and 3 * 4. Start E ⇒ E + T.

steps.title: Complete the leftmost subexpression
steps.html:
E ⇒ E + T
  ⇒ T + T
  ⇒ F + T
  ⇒ 2 + T

The T on the right remains untouched while the variables to its left are expanded.

steps.title: Finish the leftmost derivation
steps.html:
2 + T ⇒ 2 + T * F
      ⇒ 2 + F * F
      ⇒ 2 + 3 * F
      ⇒ 2 + 3 * 4

At each arrow, the selected variable is the leftmost one still present.

steps.title: Construct the rightmost derivation separately
steps.html:
E ⇒ E + T
  ⇒ E + T * F
  ⇒ E + T * 4
  ⇒ E + F * 4
  ⇒ E + 3 * 4
  ⇒ T + 3 * 4
  ⇒ F + 3 * 4
  ⇒ 2 + 3 * 4

The production structure is the same. Only the order in which its independent branches are completed changes.

practice.prompt: Give a complete derivation of 0011 using S → 0S1 | ε. Identify every sentential form.
practice.hint: Count how many applications of the recursive rule create two zeros.
practice.solution:
S ⇒ 0S1 ⇒ 00S11 ⇒ 0011

All four strings shown are sentential forms. The final one contains only terminals. There are two recursive applications and one terminating application.

practice.prompt: Using S → AB, A → aA | ε, B → bB | ε, give a leftmost derivation of aab.
practice.hint: Finish A before touching B.
practice.solution:
S ⇒ AB ⇒ aAB ⇒ aaAB ⇒ aaB ⇒ aabB ⇒ aab

The fourth arrow removes A with A → ε. The final arrow removes B. Expanding B before A disappears would break the leftmost requirement, though it could still be a valid unrestricted derivation.

check.prompt: In the sentential form aABb, which variable must a rightmost derivation expand next?
check.answer: B
check.explanation: B is the rightmost remaining variable. The terminal b to its right does not affect that choice.

transfer.prompt: Use E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → number | ( E ) to give both a leftmost and a rightmost derivation of (5 + 6) * 7. Keep every intermediate sentential form.

title: Build parse trees for expressions and programs
summary: Convert production choices into an ordered tree and check that its leaves reproduce the input.
goals: Use the start variable as the root.
Expand each variable with the exact right-hand side of one rule.
Include punctuation, list tails and epsilon leaves.
Check a complete tree by reading its yield.

sections.title: What a parse tree records
sections.html:
A parse tree records which production was used at every variable occurrence. The root is the start variable. If a node X uses X → α₁ … αₖ, its children, in that order, are α₁ … αₖ. Variables are expanded further; terminals remain leaves. An ε production is usually displayed by an ε leaf, which contributes no token to the yield.

The yield is the terminal sequence obtained by reading leaves from left to right, ignoring ε. It must exactly match the target token stream, including every bracket, parenthesis and comma.

Two valid derivations that differ only in expansion order can describe the same tree. To compare trees, compare the production structure, not the order in which you drew their branches.

sections.title: A small expression tree
sections.html:
E → E Op E | ( E ) | number
Op → + | *

For (2 + 5) * 8, the root E uses E → E Op E. Its first E expands to ( E ), its Op expands to *, and its last E expands to number 8. The E inside the parentheses expands to another E Op E, yielding 2, + and 5.

Node occurrenceProductionOrdered children
Root EE → E Op EE, Op, E
Root’s first EE → ( E )(, E, )
E inside parenthesesE → E Op EE, Op, E
Root OpOp → **

This table is a construction guide; the completed tree must also expand both Op nodes and all number-producing E nodes.

sections.title: Use explicit recursive list rules
sections.html:
Function → def id ( Params ) Block
Params → ε | id ParamTail
ParamTail → ε | , id ParamTail
Block → { Stmts }
Stmts → ε | Stmt Stmts
Stmt → If | Return
If → if ( Expr ) Block
Return → return Expr
Expr → id | id . Expr | id ( Args )
Args → ε | Expr ArgTail
ArgTail → ε | , Expr ArgTail

A block with two statements has Stmts → Stmt Stmts twice, then Stmts → ε. A single parameter still has a ParamTail node ending in ε. A one-argument call still has an ArgTail node ending in ε. Include these nodes even when nothing is visibly printed at their positions.

Use the grammar exactly as supplied. A parse tree is not a shortened abstract syntax tree: grammar variables, punctuation and empty productions remain visible.

sections.title: Add deeper nesting without changing the method
sections.html:
To add another if inside the first if, expand an inner Stmt by Stmt → If, then use If → if ( Expr ) Block. The new Block gets its own Stmts chain. Do not attach the nested if directly to the outer Function or omit the intermediate Stmt and Stmts variables.

Check each closing brace against the Block that produced it. An outer statement after the if belongs to the outer block’s remaining Stmts, not to the if’s Block.

worked.title: Construct the program tree in a controlled order
worked.intro: Use the complete grammar and probe program above. Begin with the whole function, then finish one subtree at a time.

steps.title: Draw the outer production
steps.html: Make Function the root with children def, id: probe, (, Params, ), Block in that order. This fixes the outer token sequence.

steps.title: Complete the parameter list
steps.html: Use Params → id ParamTail with id: cursor. End the tail with ParamTail → ε. A one-item list needs both nodes.

steps.title: Count the outer statements
steps.html: The outer block has an If statement and a Return statement. Use the Stmts recursion twice and terminate the last Stmts with ε. Expand the first Stmt by Stmt → If and the second by Stmt → Return.

steps.title: Expand the if and its own block
steps.html: The outer condition uses Expr → id for cursor. Its Block contains one nested If, followed by an empty Stmts tail. The nested condition uses Expr → id . Expr for cursor.link. The nested If’s own Block contains one Return, followed by another empty Stmts tail. Each if has its own (, Expr, ), Block children.

steps.title: Expand the call and member access
steps.html: The return expression uses Expr → id ( Args ) for probe. Args uses Expr ArgTail. That Expr uses id . Expr, with cursor before the dot and a final Expr → id for link. ArgTail ends with ε.

steps.title: Verify every leaf and production
steps.html: Read the yield left to right. It must be def id ( id ) { if ( id ) { if ( id . id ) { return id ( id . id ) } } return id }. Check that every internal node’s children match a rule and every remaining variable has been expanded.

practice.prompt: Using the list grammar from the previous lesson, describe every node needed to parse [ id ]. Where does ε appear?
practice.hint: A list with one item still has a tail.
practice.solution: The root S has children [, L, ]. L has children id and T. T has one ε child. The yield is [, id, ]; ε contributes no input symbol. Omitting T would skip a grammar symbol and would not be a complete parse tree.

practice.prompt: With the program grammar above, build the subtree for return cursor.link.
practice.hint: Begin at Stmt, then Return, then decide which Expr rule matches the dot.
practice.solution: Stmt has child Return. Return has children terminal return and Expr. That Expr has children id: cursor, terminal dot, and Expr. The final Expr has child id: link. No Args node appears because this is member access, not a call.

check.prompt: A Block contains three statements. How many uses of Stmts → Stmt Stmts and Stmts → ε are required?
check.answer: Three recursive uses and one epsilon use.
check.explanation: Each recursive use contributes one statement. The final Stmts must terminate, contributing no further statement.

transfer.prompt: Using the supplied program grammar, draw a complete parse tree for def select(x,y) { if (x.link) { if (y) { return select(x.link,y) } } return y }. Include all punctuation and epsilon leaves, then verify the yield.
transfer.solution: Function uses def id ( Params ) Block. Params uses id ParamTail; that tail uses , id ParamTail and then ε. The outer Block has two statements: If and Return, followed by an ε Stmts tail. The outer If condition uses Expr → id . Expr for x.link; its Block has one If statement and an ε tail. That inner If condition uses Expr → id for y; its Block has one Return and an ε tail. Its call expression uses Expr → id ( Args ). Args holds Expr for x.link, then an ArgTail using , Expr ArgTail for y, then ε. The final outer Return uses Expr → id for y. At every level, include the intermediate Stmt and Stmts nodes. Reading the leaves must reproduce the exact token sequence, with each of the three brace pairs in its own Block subtree.

title: Design grammars from constraints
summary: Choose rules that create the required structure and justify both what the grammar includes and what it excludes.
goals: Choose base cases before recursive cases.
Separate matching, independent blocks, concatenation and union.
Generate nonempty and optional components deliberately.
Explain soundness and completeness of a grammar.

sections.title: A construction method
sections.html:
1. Translate the definition into order, counts and boundary cases.
  2. List the shortest valid strings, including whether ε is allowed.
  3. Choose a variable for each independent component.
  4. Choose a recursive rule that preserves the intended relationships.
  5. Add a base case that ends every variable.
  6. Test members and near misses.
  7. Explain why every generated string is valid and every valid string can be generated.

Testing catches mistakes, but testing alone cannot prove exact language equality.

sections.title: Independent repetition and matching repetition
sections.html:
A → aA | ε
B → bB | ε
S → AB

These rules generate a*b*: the number of a symbols and the number of b symbols are independent.

S → aSb | ε

This rule generates equal block lengths. One recursive application contributes one a at the left and one b at the right. For a 1:2 ratio, use S → aSbb | ε. To require at least one matched pair, use S → aSb | ab instead.

sections.title: Build a language by combining smaller languages
sections.html:
For concatenation, use S → AB when A generates the first component and B the second. For union, use S → A | B: a derivation chooses one branch. Reuse variable names only when they represent the same intended language.

For a strict inequality of two block counts, separate a matched part from a nonempty surplus. For example, more b symbols than a symbols can be generated by matching each a with a b, then adding at least one extra b. The surplus rule must not accidentally allow ε.

sections.title: Prove the two directions
sections.html:
Soundness: show a generated string satisfies the definition. Identify what each recursive rule preserves and what the base case establishes.

Completeness: take any string satisfying the definition and explain how many times to use each rule to generate it. If the language has cases, handle each case. This prevents an appealing grammar from silently omitting valid strings.

worked.title: Generate a smaller a block followed by a larger b block
worked.intro: Design a CFG for L = {aⁱbʲ : 0 ≤ i < j}. This includes b and aabbb, but excludes ε and aabb.

steps.title: Separate equality from surplus
steps.html: Write j = i + r, where r ≥ 1. The grammar must create i matched a/b pairs and then r additional b symbols.

steps.title: Choose the matching rule
steps.html:
S → aSb | B

After i recursive uses, the form is aⁱ B bⁱ. The remaining B must generate a nonempty b string.

steps.title: Make the surplus nonempty
steps.html:
B → bB | b

B generates bʳ for r ≥ 1. Do not use B → ε here, because that would allow equality.

steps.title: Derive and reject representative strings
steps.html:
S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aaBbb ⇒ aabbb

This uses i = 2 and r = 1. b comes from S ⇒ B ⇒ b. Neither ε nor aabb can be generated because B always contributes at least one b.

steps.title: Justify exactness
steps.html: Every derivation yields aⁱbʳbⁱ = aⁱbⁱ⁺ʳ, with r ≥ 1, so it is valid. Conversely, if i < j, take r = j − i; use the matching rule i times, then generate r b symbols from B. Every valid string is covered.

practice.prompt: Design a grammar for {aⁿb²ⁿ : n ≥ 1}. Derive the case n = 2.
practice.hint: Each recursive step must create the same 1:2 ratio as the base case.
practice.solution:
S → aSbb | abb
S ⇒ aSbb ⇒ aabbbb

The base has one a and two b symbols. Every recursive use adds another a and another two b symbols, preserving the ratio and the block order.

practice.prompt: Design a grammar for strings that are either a nonempty block of a symbols or a nonempty block of b symbols, but do not mix them.
practice.hint: Use union at the start; do not concatenate the two branches.
practice.solution:
S → A | B
A → aA | a
B → bB | b

The branch chooses which symbol may occur. Both bases are nonempty, so ε is excluded. S → AB would instead force a component of each kind.

check.prompt: Why does replacing B → bB | b by B → bB | ε break the strict-inequality grammar?
check.answer: It permits zero surplus b symbols, allowing equal counts.
check.explanation: For example S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aBb ⇒ ab would then be possible, even though i < j excludes ab.

transfer.prompt: Construct and justify a CFG for {aⁱbʲ : i > j ≥ 0}. Give derivations of aaab and a. Explain soundness and completeness in terms of the surplus.
transfer.solution:
S → aSb | A
A → aA | a
S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aAb ⇒ aaAb ⇒ aaab
S ⇒ A ⇒ a

After j matched steps the form is aʲAbʲ. A contributes r ≥ 1 additional a symbols, giving aʲ⁺ʳbʲ. Thus every generated string has more a symbols. Conversely, for any i > j, use j matched steps and generate i − j a symbols from A.

title: Use recursion for nesting and balanced structure
summary: Distinguish nested matching from sequences of independently balanced components.
goals: Explain what a recursive production adds around its recursive call.
Distinguish even palindromes, equal-count blocks and balanced parentheses.
Use concatenation to generate multiple balanced components.
Design rules with paired symbols or ratio constraints.

sections.title: Three different languages, three different constraints
sections.html:
LanguageExampleUseful grammar
Equal ordered blocksaaabbbS → aSb | ε
Even-length palindromesabba, baabS → aSa | bSb | ε
Balanced parentheses(()()), ()()S → ( S ) S | ε

Each grammar has recursive dependence, but they recognize different properties. Equal counts do not imply correct nesting, and a palindrome need not have equal counts of its two symbols.

sections.title: Read outside-in rules literally
sections.html:
S → 0S0 | 1S1 | ε

At every recursive step, the left and right added symbols match. Ending with ε gives an even-length palindrome. Equivalently, the language is {wwᴿ : w ∈ {0,1}*}. The right half reverses the left half.

For example, choosing outside symbols 0, then 1, then 0 gives S ⇒ 0S0 ⇒ 01S10 ⇒ 010S010 ⇒ 010010. This is w wᴿ for w = 010. In general wwᴿ is different from ww; use w = 01 to see 0110 versus 0101.

sections.title: Balanced means every prefix is safe
sections.html:
A parentheses string is balanced when its total number of opens equals its total number of closes and every prefix has at least as many opens as closes. The string )( has equal totals but fails at its first symbol.

S → ( S ) S | ε

For every nonempty balanced string, the first opening parenthesis has a unique matching close. The first S generates the balanced contents inside that pair; the second S generates the balanced remainder after the pair. This supports nesting and side-by-side groups.

sections.title: Alternative balanced grammar and its scope
sections.html:
S → SS | ( S ) | ε

This grammar also generates all balanced parentheses strings: SS joins two balanced strings, (S) encloses one, and ε supplies the empty string. It is useful when converting CFG rules to a PDA, though it is ambiguous. For a hand-written predictive parser, the earlier S → ( S ) S | ε grammar gives cleaner choices.

The grammar S → ( S ) | ε generates only fully nested pairs: ε, (), (()), ((())), and so on. It cannot generate ()() because it has no rule that supplies a balanced remainder.

worked.title: Generate (()()) and explain both S positions
worked.intro: Use S → ( S ) S | ε. Label variable occurrences during planning so the inside and remainder are not confused.

steps.title: Split at the first matching close
steps.html: In (()()), the first opening parenthesis matches the final closing parenthesis. The inside is ()(); the remainder is ε.

steps.title: Generate the outer pair
steps.html: Use S → ( S ) S. The first variable must produce ()(), and the second must produce ε.

steps.title: Generate the two inside components
steps.html:
S ⇒ ( S ) S
  ⇒ ( ( S ) S ) S
  ⇒ ( ( ) S ) S
  ⇒ ( ( ) ( S ) S ) S

The first inside component is (). The inside remainder now generates another pair.

steps.title: Terminate every remaining variable
steps.html:
( ( ) ( S ) S ) S
⇒ ( ( ) ( ) S ) S
⇒ ( ( ) ( ) ) S
⇒ ( ( ) ( ) )

The yield is (()()). Each ε application removes exactly one variable occurrence. Every opening parenthesis has its closing partner in the same production.

practice.prompt: Which of 0110, 0101, ε and 010 are generated by S → 0S0 | 1S1 | ε?
practice.hint: Check even length and matching outside symbols.
practice.solution: 0110 and ε are generated. A derivation is S ⇒ 0S0 ⇒ 01S10 ⇒ 0110. 0101 fails because its outside symbols differ. 010 is an odd palindrome, but this grammar adds symbols in pairs and has only an even-length base.

practice.prompt: Modify the palindrome grammar to generate all palindromes over {0,1}, of both odd and even lengths.
practice.hint: Add the possible middle symbols as base cases.
practice.solution:
S → 0S0 | 1S1 | 0 | 1 | ε

The base ε gives an even-length result. Bases 0 and 1 give an odd-length result. Recursive rules still enforce matching outside symbols.

check.prompt: Why can S → (S) | ε not generate ()()?
check.answer: Every nonempty derivation has one outer pair enclosing the entire remaining string.
check.explanation: The first opening parenthesis must match the last closing parenthesis in every generated nonempty string, which is false for ()().

transfer.prompt: Give a grammar for properly balanced strings using two kinds of brackets, () and []. It must allow interleaving of balanced components and nesting of either type inside the other. Derive [()].
transfer.solution:
S → ( S ) S | [ S ] S | ε
S ⇒ [ S ] S ⇒ [ ( S ) S ] S ⇒ [ ( ) S ] S ⇒ [ ( ) ] S ⇒ [ ( ) ]

Each recursive production supplies one correctly matched outer pair, balanced contents, and a balanced remainder. The grammar rejects ([)] because no production can make an opening bracket close with a different type.

title: Resolve ambiguity, precedence and associativity
summary: Use parse-tree structure to explain which operations bind together and how to make the intended grouping explicit.
goals: Recognize ambiguity by two distinct parse trees for one string.
Distinguish ambiguity from different derivation orders.
Use expression, term and factor levels for precedence.
State whether a grammar feature is suitable for predictive parsing.

sections.title: Ambiguity is about more than one tree
sections.html:
E → E + E | E * E | number

The token sequence 2 + 3 * 4 can have a + root, meaning 2 + (3 * 4), or a * root, meaning (2 + 3) * 4. These are different parse trees with the same yield. Therefore this grammar is ambiguous.

A leftmost and rightmost derivation of the same tree do not establish ambiguity. A reliable demonstration gives two different trees or two different leftmost derivations of one terminal string.

This lesson extends the slides’ arithmetic examples. The grammar in the initial examples describes permitted expression syntax without itself resolving all grouping choices.

sections.title: Encode precedence in separate variable levels
sections.html:
E → E + T | E - T | T
T → T * F | T / F | F
F → number | id | ( E )

E is an expression, T a term, and F a factor. Multiplication and division are completed inside T before the enclosing E combines terms with addition or subtraction. Parentheses create a factor containing a whole E, so they override the usual precedence.

For 2 + 3 * 4, the root E uses E → E + T. Its right T can generate 3 * 4. The grammar cannot make + occur inside an unparenthesized factor, so the alternative grouping is excluded.

sections.title: Associativity determines equal-precedence grouping
sections.html:
For subtraction, (8 - 3) - 1 = 4, while 8 - (3 - 1) = 6. The rule E → E - T makes repeated subtraction left-associative: the left E may contain the preceding subtraction. A grammar with E → T - E | T instead permits a subtraction chain nested on the right.

Precedence answers which kinds of operations group first. Associativity answers how a sequence of operations at the same precedence groups.

sections.title: A related program ambiguity: optional else
sections.html:
Stmt → if ( Expr ) Stmt
     | if ( Expr ) Stmt else Stmt
     | other

In if (a) if (b) x else y, the else can be attached to the inner if or the outer if. A language must define a rule, commonly attaching else to the nearest unmatched if, or use explicit blocks that make the grouping clear.

One grammar repair separates matched statements from unmatched ones. Another language design requires braces for both branches. This topic is supplementary: do not silently change a supplied grammar when asked to draw one of its parse trees.

sections.title: Left recursion and predictive parsing
sections.html:
E → E + T is directly left recursive because the right-hand side begins with E. A naive recursive descent procedure that immediately calls parse_E again consumes no token and can recurse forever.

E → T E′
E′ → + T E′ | - T E′ | ε

This removes the direct left recursion for the addition/subtraction level. A parser should accumulate operations from left to right when building a left-associative expression tree. Merely changing the grammar’s shape is not enough to justify silently changing the meaning of subtraction.

worked.title: Show two groupings, then choose a grammar that fixes them
worked.intro: Compare an unrestricted arithmetic grammar with the E/T/F grammar for the same input 2 + 3 * 4.

steps.title: Make the + root
steps.html: Under E → E + E | E * E | number, choose E → E + E at the root. The right E uses E → E * E. The yield is 2 + 3 * 4 with multiplication grouped on the right.

steps.title: Make the * root
steps.html: Choose E → E * E at the root. Its left E uses E → E + E. The same yield is produced with addition grouped on the left.

steps.title: State why this proves ambiguity
steps.html: The root productions differ, so the parse trees differ. Since both have the same terminal yield, one string has two distinct parse trees.

steps.title: Apply the precedence grammar
steps.html: Using E/T/F, the root addition combines a left E for 2 with a right T for 3 * 4. A multiplication root at the term level cannot contain an unparenthesized addition in either factor. Only the intended grouping remains.

practice.prompt: For E → E - E | number, describe two parse trees for 9 - 4 - 2 and give the value associated with each.
practice.hint: Choose whether the first or second minus is the root operation.
practice.solution: A root minus with left subtree 9 - 4 gives (9 - 4) - 2 = 3. A root minus with right subtree 4 - 2 gives 9 - (4 - 2) = 7. The grammar is ambiguous because these distinct trees share a yield.

practice.prompt: In the E/T/F grammar above, explain the grouping of 8 - 3 - 1. Then explain how 8 - (3 - 1) becomes possible.
practice.hint: The right side of E → E - T is a T. A parenthesized E can appear inside a factor.
practice.solution: The unparenthesized chain groups (8 - 3) - 1 because the left E contains the earlier subtraction. For the second input, the right T becomes F and F → ( E ); that inner E generates 3 - 1. Parentheses explicitly permit the otherwise unavailable right-hand subtraction.

check.prompt: Does finding one leftmost and one rightmost derivation of a string prove ambiguity?
check.answer: No. They can be two construction orders for the same tree.
check.explanation: Ambiguity requires two different parse trees, or equivalently two different leftmost derivations of one string.

transfer.prompt: Design expression grammar levels for + and * where * has higher precedence, and parentheses can override it. Explain the parse of a * (b + c) + d. Identify any direct left recursion and explain what a naive recursive descent parser would do.
transfer.solution:
E → E + T | T
T → T * F | F
F → id | ( E )

The root E combines the term a * (b + c) with d. Its multiplication is inside the left term; the parenthesized sum is an F containing an inner E. The E and T rules are directly left recursive. A naive procedure following them can call itself without consuming input; transform them to tail rules or use another suitable parsing approach.

title: Parse with lookahead, a table and a stack
summary: Follow an LL(1) parser from tokens to a tree, then express the same decisions as recursive descent.
goals: Decode LL(k) and LR(k).
Choose productions from disjoint predictor sets.
Trace a predictive parser with stack and remaining input.
Reject both missing tokens and extra tokens.
Compare an explicit parser stack with recursive descent.

sections.title: Where parsing belongs
sections.html:
A scanner converts source characters into tokens. A parser checks the token sequence against the grammar and constructs a parse tree. Later compiler phases analyze meaning and generate executable code. A parser is responsible for structural syntax, not for deciding whether a variable exists or whether every operation is type-correct.

For total + 12, the scanner can produce id, +, integer, retaining total and 12 as lexemes. The parser decides how those tokens fit the grammar.

sections.title: Read LL(k) and LR(k)
sections.html:
NameInput directionDerivation/tree constructionk
LL(k)Left to rightLeftmost derivation; usually top downNumber of lookahead tokens
LR(k)Left to rightRightmost derivation reconstructed in reverse; bottom upNumber of lookahead tokens

LL(1) uses one lookahead token to choose the next production for the current variable. This is a restriction on the grammar: not every CFG permits that choice. LR parsing is not a right-to-left scan of the input.

sections.title: A complete predictive grammar and table
sections.html:
S → + S S | - S S | * S S | / S S | integer

This is prefix notation: an operator is followed by exactly two expressions. For example + 2 * 3 4 means 2 + (3 * 4).

VariableLookahead / predictor setSelected production
S{+}S → + S S
S{-}S → - S S
S{*}S → * S S
S{/}S → / S S
S{integer}S → integer

Predictor sets for alternatives with the same left side must be disjoint. When S is on top and lookahead is +, the parser has one permitted choice. An unlisted token is a syntax error.

sections.title: The iterative algorithm, with complete acceptance conditions
sections.html:
Use an end marker $ that is not an ordinary input token. Put S $ on the stack with the top written on the left; append $ to the input.

  1. If the top is a variable, use its table row and the current lookahead to choose a production. Replace that variable by the right-hand side, with its first symbol becoming the new top.
  2. If the top is a terminal equal to lookahead, pop it and advance one input token.
  3. If the top is a mismatching terminal, or a table entry is missing, reject.
  4. Accept only when the stack and input both reach their end markers together.

When implementing a physical stack by individual push operations, push the right-hand side in reverse order. For S → + S S, push the last S, then the first S, then +. The next popped symbol is +.

Do not accept merely because all input tokens were consumed: the stack might still require another operand. Do not accept merely because the grammar part of the stack is empty: unread input might remain.

sections.title: Recursive descent makes the same decisions
sections.html:
parse_S():
  t = lookahead()
  if t is integer:
    consume(integer)
    return node(S, t)
  if t is one of +, -, *, /:
    consume(t)
    left = parse_S()
    right = parse_S()
    return node(S, t, left, right)
  syntax_error()

parse_program():
  tree = parse_S()
  require_end_of_input()
  return tree

The procedure call stack stores the pending expressions. An iterative parser stores them explicitly. Both select the same productions from the same lookahead information. A full tree can retain intermediate variables such as Add when the grammar has S → Add and Add → + S S.

sections.title: Extension: epsilon predictions, FIRST and FOLLOW
sections.html:
The slides provide predictor sets directly. To compute them in a larger grammar, FIRST(α) records which terminals can begin strings derived from α. If α can derive ε, also consider FOLLOW(A): tokens allowed immediately after A.

List → [ Items ]
Items → integer Tail | ε
Tail → , integer Tail | ε

For Items, lookahead integer selects the nonempty rule; lookahead ] selects ε. For Tail, comma selects another item; ] selects ε. ε itself is not a lookahead token. If two productions for one variable predict the same lookahead, the table has a conflict and is not LL(1) as written.

A common cause is a shared prefix, as in A → id | id ( Args ). One token id cannot decide between them. Left factoring can expose the later decision: A → id Rest, Rest → ( Args ) | ε, provided the rest of the grammar supplies suitable, nonconflicting predictions for ε.

worked.title: Trace a predictive parser on + 2 * 3 4
worked.intro: The stack top is on the left. Input and stack both include the end marker $. Every row below records the state before the listed action.

steps.title: Expand the first expression
steps.html:
StackRemaining inputAction
S $+ 2 * 3 4 $S → + S S
+ S S $+ 2 * 3 4 $Match +
S S $2 * 3 4 $S → integer
integer S $2 * 3 4 $Match integer 2

steps.title: Expand the second operand
steps.html:
StackRemaining inputAction
S $* 3 4 $S → * S S
* S S $* 3 4 $Match *
S S $3 4 $S → integer
integer S $3 4 $Match integer 3

steps.title: Finish the final operand
steps.html:
StackRemaining inputAction
S $4 $S → integer
integer $4 $Match integer 4
$$Accept

Both completion conditions hold. The root is +; its left child expression is 2, and its right child expression is * 3 4.

steps.title: Test nearby invalid inputs
steps.html: For + 2, another S remains when lookahead is $, so reject: one operand is missing. For + 2 3 4, the stack reaches $ while lookahead is integer 4, so reject: an extra token remains. These are different failure conditions.

practice.prompt: Trace the prefix input * + 1 2 3 using the table. Which operator is the root, and which expression is its first operand?
practice.hint: Choose a rule from the next token each time S reaches the top.
practice.solution: The root is *. Its first operand is + 1 2; its second operand is 3. The production sequence is S → *SS, first S → +SS, then integer for 1, integer for 2, and integer for 3. The parser alternates these expansions with terminal matches and accepts only when both end markers are reached.

practice.prompt: For the List/Items/Tail grammar, choose the production when Items sees ], when Tail sees comma, and when Tail sees integer. Explain the last case.
practice.hint: An epsilon alternative applies only on tokens allowed after the variable.
practice.solution: Items with ] uses Items → ε. Tail with comma uses Tail → , integer Tail. Tail with integer is an error: another item requires a separating comma, and ] is the permitted following token for the ε choice. Choosing ε for every unknown token would hide syntax errors.

check.prompt: A parser stack has only $, but the input still has integer 7 followed by $. Should it accept?
check.answer: No. There is unread input.
check.explanation: A successful parse consumes one complete start-symbol string and reaches input and stack end markers together.

transfer.prompt: Write recursive descent pseudocode for List → [ Items ], Items → integer Tail | ε, Tail → , integer Tail | ε. Use ] as the epsilon prediction. Explain how [ integer , ] is rejected.
transfer.solution:
parse_List():
  consume([)
  parse_Items()
  consume(])

parse_Items():
  if lookahead() is integer:
    consume(integer)
    parse_Tail()
  else if lookahead() == ]:
    return
  else: syntax_error()

parse_Tail():
  if lookahead() == ,:
    consume(,)
    consume(integer)
    parse_Tail()
  else if lookahead() == ]:
    return
  else: syntax_error()

After a comma, consume(integer) is mandatory. Seeing ] at that position causes an error before parse_Tail can choose its ε branch. The top-level caller also checks that no token remains after the closing ].

title: Read a PDA one transition at a time
summary: Track the state, unread input, and stack separately before designing a machine.
goals: Read every part of a transition label.
Distinguish input symbols, stack symbols, and states.
Write a complete configuration trace.

sections.title: Start with one complete machine
sections.html:
A pushdown automaton (PDA) has finite control and a stack. For {xⁿyⁿ : n ≥ 0}, the state records whether we are reading x symbols or y symbols. The stack records how many x symbols still need matching y symbols. Before choosing transitions, decide what one stack symbol means.

Use input alphabet Σ = {x,y}, stack alphabet Γ = {A,Z}, and initial stack Z. Here A means one unmatched x. Z is a bottom marker, not an input character. A stack can contain many copies of A even though Γ is a finite set.

sections.title: Fix the stack convention
sections.html:
We write the top of the stack on the left. Therefore AAZ has an A on top and Z at the bottom. Pushing B gives BAAZ; popping B restores AAZ. If a diagram draws its stack vertically, the same contents have B at the top.

A configuration is (state, unread input, stack). For example, (push, xyyy, AAZ) records three separate facts. It does not mean that xyyy is on the stack.

sections.title: Read input, pop, push
sections.html:
The slides write a transition as input,pop/push. Read those fields in that order. A label y,A/ε consumes the next y and removes the top A. It is disabled if the next input is x or the top is Z. A label ε,A/ε removes A without consuming input. A label x,ε/A consumes x and pushes A without popping.

The three ε symbols have different positions and therefore different effects: ε in the input field means consume nothing; ε in the pop field means do not inspect or remove a stack symbol in the slide shorthand; ε in the push field means push nothing. ε is not a literal character to type in the input.

In a top-inspecting convention, push A above T is written x,T/AT, for each possible top T. Our tables use that explicit form when top checks matter. Replacing A by AA increases the number of A symbols by one: remove the old A, then put two As in its place.

sections.title: Name the seven parts
sections.html:
A PDA is written M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, Z, F). Q is the finite set of states; Σ is the input alphabet; Γ is the stack alphabet; δ is the transition relation; q₀ is the start state; Z is the initial stack symbol; F is the set of accepting states when using final-state acceptance.

An NPDA can have several possible next configurations. A string is accepted if at least one complete branch accepts. Do not combine the stack from one branch with the state from another branch.

worked.title: Trace xxyy
worked.intro: Use states push and pop. On x, push one A. On the first y, move to pop and remove one A. Later y symbols each remove one A. Finishing acceptance is examined in the next lesson.

steps.title: Write the initial configuration
steps.html:
(push, xxyy, Z)

No input has been consumed. Z is the whole stack.

steps.title: Read the first x
steps.html:
Apply x,Z/AZ.

(push, xyy, AZ)

One x has been consumed and one x remains unmatched.

steps.title: Read the second x
steps.html:
Apply x,A/AA.

(push, yy, AAZ)

The stack contains two unmatched-x markers.

steps.title: Read and match the first y
steps.html:
Move to pop using y,A/ε.

(pop, y, AZ)

The unread suffix loses one y, and the stack loses one A.

steps.title: Read and match the final y
steps.html:
Apply the pop-state loop y,A/ε.

(pop, ε, Z)

Every input symbol has been consumed, and no unmatched x markers remain. Z is still present.

practice.prompt: Starting at (q, yx, BAZ), apply y,B/ε to state r. What is the new configuration?
practice.hint: Update each of the three fields once.
practice.solution: (r, x, AZ). Consume y, remove the top B, and change the state to r. The A and Z remain.

practice.prompt: Starting at (q, xy, AZ), apply ε,A/BA to state r. What changes?
practice.hint: The ε is in the input field, not the push field.
practice.solution: The result is (r, xy, BAZ). The input is unchanged. Replace top A by BA, so B is the new top. Z remains below the replacement.

practice.prompt: Why is y,A/ε disabled at (q, y, Z)?
practice.hint: A transition must satisfy its stack guard.
practice.solution: The top is Z, but the transition requires A. The machine cannot pop an A from below or invent one. This is how the stack prevents an extra y from matching a nonexistent x.

check.prompt: In the convention used here, which end of AAZ is the top?
check.answer: The left end.
check.explanation: The next pop removes the leftmost A. State the convention before tracing any multi-symbol push.

transfer.prompt: Trace xxxyyy until the stack contains only Z. Give all configurations and state what A counts.
transfer.solution:
(push, xxxyyy, Z)
(push, xxyyy, AZ)
(push, xyyy, AAZ)
(push, yyy, AAAZ)
(pop, yy, AAZ)
(pop, y, AZ)
(pop, ε, Z)

Each A counts one x that has already been read but has not yet been matched by a y.

title: Finish a run: acceptance and the bottom marker
summary: Make full input consumption and the chosen acceptance rule explicit.
goals: Apply final-state and empty-stack acceptance correctly.
Use a bottom marker to detect completed matching.
Explain rejection using an unread symbol or unmatched stack symbol.

sections.title: Two acceptance rules
sections.html:
ModeRequired at the end of one branchMay remain
Final stateAll input consumed and current state is in FStack symbols, including Z
Empty stackAll input consumed and stack emptyAny state

Reaching a final state with unread input does not accept the whole string. Emptying the stack with unread input does not accept the whole string either. An NPDA accepts when at least one branch reaches the required ending configuration.

sections.title: What the bottom marker tells us
sections.html:
For a counter stack AᵏZ, seeing Z on top means k = 0. Seeing A means a match is still required. The marker is useful because a transition can explicitly test Z; a transition that simply ignores the stack cannot test that all As have been removed.

Under final-state acceptance, Z can remain. Under empty-stack acceptance, a successful branch must eventually remove Z. Thus a diagram that leaves Z behind can be correct for final-state acceptance and incorrect for empty-stack acceptance.

sections.title: A precise finishing rule for xⁿyⁿ
sections.html:
Use start state push, second state pop, and halt state done. Let done have no outgoing transitions. In push, reading x pushes A. Reading the first y requires A, removes it, and enters pop. In pop, each y removes A; no transition reads x.

For empty-stack acceptance, add ε,Z/ε from push to done for the n = 0 case and from pop to done for completed positive cases. An early branch that removes Z while input remains stops and rejects. These ε choices make this construction nondeterministic under standard DPDA rules; it is an NPDA.

For final-state acceptance, replace those finishing transitions by ε,Z/Z to an accepting done state. The stack ends as Z. The equivalence of the modes is a statement about NPDAs; deterministic restrictions require separate care.

sections.title: Prove what the stack means
sections.html:
An invariant is a statement preserved by the transitions. In push, after reading xᵏ the stack is AᵏZ. In pop, after reading xⁿyʲ the stack is Aⁿ⁻ʲZ, with 0 < j ≤ n. Since no x is permitted in pop, the order is x* y*. The final Z test gives j = n.

This proves both directions: every accepted string has the required order and equal counts; for every n ≥ 0, the intended run reads xⁿyⁿ and finishes. Testing examples is useful, but this invariant explains all lengths.

worked.title: Compare three endings
worked.intro: Use the empty-stack NPDA described above. Track full configurations, including the finishing transition.

steps.title: Accept a positive example
steps.html:
(push, xxyy, Z) → (push, xyy, AZ)
→ (push, yy, AAZ) → (pop, y, AZ)
→ (pop, ε, Z) → (done, ε, ε)

The last move is ε,Z/ε. Both acceptance conditions hold.

steps.title: Handle the empty string
steps.html:
(push, ε, Z) → (done, ε, ε)

The language allows n = 0, so the machine must accept ε.

steps.title: Reject too few y symbols
steps.html:
(push, xxy, Z) → (push, xy, AZ)
→ (push, y, AAZ) → (pop, ε, AZ)

Input is finished, but A remains. The finishing move requires Z on top, so this branch cannot accept.

steps.title: Reject too many y symbols
steps.html:
(push, xyy, Z) → (push, yy, AZ)
→ (pop, y, Z) → (done, y, ε)

This branch has an empty stack but unread y. done has no outgoing transitions. There is no accepting branch.

steps.title: Reject the wrong order
steps.html: For xyxy, the first y moves to pop. The next x has no transition from pop. Equal total counts do not repair the invalid order.

practice.prompt: An accepting state is reached with unread suffix xy and stack Z. Has this run accepted the original input?
practice.hint: Check input consumption before looking at stack acceptance.
practice.solution: No. Final-state acceptance also requires the entire input to be consumed. If there are later transitions they may continue the run; the current configuration is not yet an accepting configuration for the whole input.

practice.prompt: A branch finishes at (q, ε, Z). Is it accepted under empty-stack acceptance? Under final-state acceptance?
practice.hint: The two modes have different requirements.
practice.solution: Empty-stack: no, because Z remains. Final-state: yes exactly when q ∈ F. Stack contents do not matter in that mode.

practice.prompt: Why must the transition that removes Z lead to a state with no input-reading transitions in our NPDA?
practice.hint: Consider removing Z before the input ends.
practice.solution: It prevents an early marker-removal branch from continuing to consume unrelated symbols and accidentally accepting. An early guess then has unread input and no continuation, so it rejects.

check.prompt: Does empty-stack acceptance allow unread input?
check.answer: No.
check.explanation: The accepting configuration must have both unread input ε and stack ε.

transfer.prompt: Design a final-state NPDA for {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}. Explain exactly how it excludes ε.
transfer.solution: Use push, pop, and accepting done. Start with Z. Push A for each a. On the first b, require A, pop it, and enter pop. Pop A on each later b. Only pop has ε,Z/Z to done. done has no outgoing transitions. There is no start-state finishing move, so reaching done requires at least one b and therefore at least one a. Accept only when the input is also exhausted.

title: Combine independent parts and nested parts
summary: Use the slides’ two patterns to turn a language description into a grammar and a PDA plan.
goals: Distinguish Pattern 1 from Pattern 2 using dependencies.
Combine grammar components without introducing unwanted dependencies.
Specify safe stack conditions at a PDA handoff.

sections.title: Pattern 1: independent concatenation
sections.html:
Pattern 1 in the slides is w = στ, where the choice of σ does not constrain the choice of τ. For {aⁿbⁿcᵐdᵐ : n,m ≥ 0}, choose a complete a/b part and then independently choose a complete c/d part. The two counts n and m may differ.

S → X Y
X → a X b | ε
Y → c Y d | ε

S → XY expresses concatenation. It does not compare the number of X expansions with the number of Y expansions. A terminal-only base production is also classified as Pattern 1 in the slide terminology.

sections.title: Pattern 2: dependent nesting
sections.html:
Pattern 2 is w = σleft τ σright, with a dependency between the left and right parts. For {aⁿ # bⁿ : n ≥ 0}, each a on the left requires a b on the right. The middle # does not affect n.

S → a S b | #

Each recursive use adds one symbol to each side. The base production supplies the middle. A PDA pushes information for the left part, processes the middle, then removes that information while reading the right part.

sections.title: Alternation and repetition
sections.html:
Alternation uses several productions with the same left side: C → c | d. Repetition uses recursion plus a stopping production: R → a R | ε for zero or more; R → a R | a for one or more.

For equal-length blocks with variable letters, use S → X S Y | ε, X → a | b, Y → c | d. This gives {uv : u ∈ {a,b}*, v ∈ {c,d}*, |u| = |v|}. The dependency is length, not identical symbol values.

sections.title: Compose PDAs with contracts
sections.html:
For independent concatenation, complete the first component before starting the next. Both components can use a protected bottom marker Z. At the handoff, require Z on top and keep it: ε,Z/Z. A generic ε,ε/ε handoff does not check that earlier obligations are finished.

For nesting, preserve outer stack information while handling the inner component. Use different marker types A and B, so the inner component removes only Bs and stops when it sees A or Z. A component contract should state its permitted input block, what it pushes, what it pops, and what must remain at exit.

These patterns are useful design methods. Merely calling a language “nested” is not a proof that a proposed grammar generates exactly that language; check its base and recursive productions.

worked.title: Build two independent matched blocks
worked.intro: Construct a grammar and a PDA plan for aⁿbⁿcᵐdᵐ, allowing either count to be zero.

steps.title: Mark the dependencies
steps.html: Match a with b, and c with d. There is no relationship between a-count and c-count. Therefore the outer structure is Pattern 1, and each matched block is Pattern 2.

steps.title: Write grammar components
steps.html:
S → X Y
X → a X b | ε
Y → c Y d | ε

X and Y independently choose how often to recurse.

steps.title: Generate one complete example
steps.html:
S ⇒ X Y ⇒ a X b Y ⇒ a a X b b Y
⇒ a a b b Y ⇒ a a b b c Y d
⇒ a a b b c d

The result has n = 2 and m = 1. Different count values are intentional.

steps.title: Give the PDA phases
steps.html: Phase a pushes A. Phase b pops A. The first component can finish only when Z is visible. Phase c pushes B. Phase d pops B. The whole machine finishes only when Z is visible again and the entire input is consumed. Use nondeterministic ε phase changes where a block may be empty.

steps.title: Test component boundaries
steps.html: Accept aabbcd, aabb, ccdd, and ε. Reject abbcd because the first match fails; reject aabbcdd because the second match fails; reject acbd because the block order is wrong.

practice.prompt: Classify aⁿbᵐcᵐdⁿ. Which dependency is processed first by the stack?
practice.hint: Write the order in which matching blocks close.
practice.solution: The a/d dependency is outer Pattern 2, and b/c is inner Pattern 2. Push A for a, then B for b. Pop B for c before popping A for d. The inner dependency closes first.

practice.prompt: Give a grammar for aⁿbⁿ followed by any number of c symbols.
practice.hint: Use one matched component and one repetition component.
practice.solution:
S → X C
X → a X b | ε
C → c C | ε

The count of c symbols is independent of the count of matched a/b pairs. In a PDA, switch to the c loop only after the a/b obligations are complete.

practice.prompt: What is wrong with a handoff that allows the second component to start while A remains?
practice.hint: State the meaning of A.
practice.solution: A represents an unfinished first-component match. Starting the next component would abandon a dependency, possibly admitting a string with too few b symbols. Require the first component’s boundary condition before handing off.

check.prompt: In these slides, which pattern is σ τ with independent choices?
check.answer: Pattern 1.
check.explanation: Pattern 2 is the dependent left/middle/right nesting pattern.

transfer.prompt: Build a grammar for aⁿ bᵐ # cᵐ dⁿ with n,m ≥ 0, and state a PDA invariant.
transfer.solution:
S → a S d | T
T → b T c | #

While reading the left blocks, the stack is BᵐAⁿZ. After #, each c removes B; d symbols can begin only after all Bs are gone. Each d then removes A. Finishing requires only Z to remain. The marker makes the middle visible; the nested order makes one stack sufficient.

title: Design ordered counts, ratios, and unequal blocks
summary: Separate block order from numeric relationships, then encode each requirement.
goals: Turn count relationships into recursive productions.
Handle zero, positive, strict, and non-strict cases.
Split an unequal-count language into two simpler cases.

sections.title: Start with the domain and order
sections.html:
{xⁿyᵐ : n,m ≥ 0} contains only an x block followed by a y block. It excludes yx even when its total counts satisfy a later equation. Write domain restrictions explicitly: n ≥ 0 allows no xs; n ≥ 1 requires at least one x.

A useful construction procedure is: state the order; identify the count relation; choose a base case; choose one recursive step; then verify what repeated steps produce.

sections.title: Fixed ratios
sections.html:
For {x²ⁿy³ⁿ : n ≥ 0}, treat one recursion as adding two xs and three ys:

S → x x S y y y | ε

After k recursive uses, there are 2k xs and 3k ys. The base ε adds neither. Positive n uses base xxyyy instead of ε.

For {xⁿy²ⁿ}, one x creates two future y obligations. A PDA may push two As for every x and remove one A per y. If a simulator permits only one-symbol pushes, use an intermediate state to perform the additional push; that state must not read another input symbol.

sections.title: At most and at least
sections.html:
For {xʲyᵏ : 0 ≤ j ≤ k}, match every x with one y and then permit extra ys:

S → x S y | Y
Y → y Y | ε

Choosing S → xSy j times and Y → yY r times gives xʲyʲ⁺ʳ, so k = j + r. For strict j < k, replace Y’s base ε by y. Then at least one extra y is required.

For {xʲyᵏ : 0 ≤ k ≤ j}, reverse where the extras occur:

S → x S y | X
X → x X | ε

This gives xᵏ⁺ʳyᵏ. If a condition also requires k ≥ 1, force one matched pair before permitting the base. Do not infer positivity from an inequality alone.

sections.title: Unequal means two strict cases
sections.html:
For n ≠ m, exactly one of n > m or n < m holds. Build one component for each and take their union:

S → U | V
U → x U y | X
X → x X | x
V → x V y | Y
Y → y Y | y

U generates xᵏ⁺ʳyᵏ with r ≥ 1; V generates xᵏyᵏ⁺ʳ with r ≥ 1. The positive base is essential: using ε in both X and Y would admit equal counts.

For an NPDA, branch at the start into “extra x” and “extra y” components. Each must enforce x* y* and demonstrate at least one surplus. A branch that merely detects that something went wrong is not enough; it still must consume the complete input in the required order.

sections.title: A complete PDA for unequal ordered counts
sections.html:
Each row is one complete transition: read the input field, require and remove the top symbol in the pop field, put the push string in its place, then enter the next state. ε in Read consumes no input; ε in Push inserts nothing. In these tables the pop field always names a real symbol, so every main-machine transition explicitly checks the top. Write stack strings with the top on the left. Any transition not listed is forbidden.

For the stated empty-stack NPDA, configure the initial stack as exactly one Z. Acceptance requires both all input consumed and stack empty. The done state has no outgoing transitions. This nonempty initial stack is necessary: neither target language here includes ε, and a truly empty initial stack would already satisfy ordinary empty-stack acceptance on ε before any transition.

If the simulator cannot preload Z and must start with an empty stack, use a fresh init state with ε,ε/Z to the listed start state and select final-state acceptance with done as the sole accepting state. Do not select ordinary empty-stack acceptance for that empty-initial-stack adapter. The initialization row uses the slide convention ε in Pop = do not pop or inspect. Every successful run reaches done with an empty stack by construction, but it is the final-state condition that prevents a zero-step acceptance at init.

This machine recognizes {xⁿyᵐ : n,m ≥ 0 and n ≠ m}. Start state start branches to the n > m component moreX or the n < m component moreY. A means one previously read x that has not been paired with y. The branches preserve the same input rather than consuming separate substrings.

Current stateReadPopPushNext state
startεZZmoreX
startεZZmoreY
moreXxZAZmoreX
moreXxAAAmoreX
moreXyAεmatchX
matchXyAεmatchX
moreXεAεdrainX
matchXεAεdrainX
drainXεAεdrainX
drainXεZεdone
moreYxZAZmoreY
moreYxAAAmoreY
moreYyAεmatchY
matchYyAεmatchY
